verses.text: Joseph was brought down to Egypt. Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh’s, the captain of the guard, an Egyptian, bought him from the hand of the Ishmaelites that had brought him down there.
Yahweh was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man. He was in the house of his master the Egyptian.
His master saw that Yahweh was with him, and that Yahweh made all that he did prosper in his hand.
Joseph found favor in his sight. He ministered to him, and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand.

From the time that he made him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, Yahweh blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake. Yahweh’s blessing was on all that he had, in the house and in the field.
He left all that he had in Joseph’s hand. He didn’t concern himself with anything, except for the food which he ate. Joseph was well-built and handsome.
After these things, his master’s wife set her eyes on Joseph; and she said, “Lie with me.”
But he refused, and said to his master’s wife, “Behold, my master doesn’t know what is with me in the house, and he has put all that he has into my hand.
No one is greater in this house than I am, and he has not kept back anything from me but you, because you are his wife. How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?”
As she spoke to Joseph day by day, he didn’t listen to her, to lie by her, or to be with her.
About this time, he went into the house to do his work, and there were none of the men of the house inside.
She caught him by his garment, saying, “Lie with me!” He left his garment in her hand, and ran outside.
When she saw that he had left his garment in her hand, and had run outside,
she called to the men of her house, and spoke to them, saying, “Behold, he has brought in a Hebrew to us to mock us. He came in to me to lie with me, and I cried with a loud voice.
When he heard that I lifted up my voice and cried, he left his garment by me, and ran outside.”
She laid up his garment by her, until his master came home.
She spoke to him according to these words, saying, “The Hebrew servant, whom you have brought to us, came in to me to mock me,
and as I lifted up my voice and cried, he left his garment by me, and ran outside.”
When his master heard the words of his wife, which she spoke to him, saying, “This is what your servant did to me,” his wrath was kindled.
Joseph’s master took him, and put him into the prison, the place where the king’s prisoners were bound, and he was there in custody.
But Yahweh was with Joseph, and showed kindness to him, and gave him favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison.
The keeper of the prison committed to Joseph’s hand all the prisoners who were in the prison. Whatever they did there, he was responsible for it.
The keeper of the prison didn’t look after anything that was under his hand, because Yahweh was with him; and that which he did, Yahweh made it prosper.

footnotes.content: The chapter picks up the sentence left hanging back in chapter 37, and the narrator gives us the whole chain: Joseph brought down, Potiphar the Egyptian, an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard, and the Ishmaelites who handed him over. It reads like a receipt, as if to say this was no rumor but a transaction with names and ranks attached. God is not mentioned once in this verse, and a young man's entire future seems to fit inside another man's hand. Hold that thought until verse 2.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Then comes the sentence the whole chapter rests on: Yahweh was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man. Notice the order. The presence is announced before the prosperity, and the prosperity is measured inside a slave's small sphere, a house that belonged to somebody else. Being with God did not keep him out of the caravan; it walked with him through it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: It is the Egyptian who sees it first. Potiphar watches this foreign servant and concludes that his God is the reason the accounts keep coming out right. A man outside the covenant is reading the evidence of a life, and he is not wrong. Most of us will never preach to a neighbor, but they will watch how we work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Potiphar stops managing his own estate and puts all of it into Joseph's hand, so the man with no property of his own runs a rich man's household. Favor like that can spoil a person, and it can also be a test with no guardrail. He was faithful over a little, and more was laid on him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now the blessing starts to spill. The Egyptian's house and fields are blessed for the sake of a Hebrew slave, which is the old promise to Abraham working quietly in a land that did not know God's name, blessing the nations through one man. Joseph is not blessed in isolation. Everyone near him gets wet from the same rain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The narrator slips in a line that sounds like an aside: Joseph was well-built and handsome. It is the very description given to his mother Rachel, and it tells us he was not only capable but noticeable, which in a house like this is dangerous. Potiphar, meanwhile, is so much at ease that he concerns himself with nothing but his own dinner. Both facts are about to matter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After these things, without any warning, the master's wife sets her eyes on him and says it plainly: lie with me. There is no courtship in it, no pretense of affection, only a command from a woman who holds power over a slave. Temptation in Scripture often comes like this, sudden, flattering, and dressed in somebody else's authority.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph refuses, and the first thing out of his mouth is not a rule but a relationship. My master does not know what is in this house, he says, because he has put it all in my hand. He argues from gratitude and from the trust he was given. A faithful man is protected by what he has been entrusted with, not only by what he has been forbidden.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He saves his strongest word for the end: how can I do this great wickedness and sin against God? Nobody is watching, no statute has been written about this yet, and the woman has every advantage over him. Still he calls the thing what it is and puts God first among the injured. That is a conscience still awake and still answering to Someone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She does not give up. She comes at him day after day, and the text says he would not listen, would not lie beside her, would not even be with her. Refusing once is a moment; refusing daily is a habit, and Joseph seems to have learned to keep his distance where argument would not help. Some battles are won by leaving the room.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One day he goes into the house to do his work, and it happens that none of the men are inside. The trap is set in the middle of ordinary duty; he was not loafing where he had no business, he was at his post. Faithfulness does not exempt a person from ambush, and it did not exempt him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She catches his garment and he runs, leaving the cloth in her hand. It is the second time a piece of Joseph's clothing has been torn off him and carried away as evidence, the first being the tunic his brothers took before they threw him in the pit. Both times the garment ends up in someone else's hands and a story gets told about him. He keeps losing the cloth and keeping his integrity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She looks down at the garment in her hand and begins to build her story on it. A scrap of cloth becomes a witness, then an accusation, then a case. What she could not get from him by asking, she will now take by lying.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She calls the men of the house and tells them a Hebrew came in to mock them, turning a private refusal into a tribal insult. The word Hebrew is old and honorable, the word used of Abraham by the oaks of Mamre, and here it is used as a slur to gather a crowd. Notice the sly turn in he has brought in, as though her husband were the one on trial.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Then she rehearses the cry she never truly cried, adding the loud voice for effect. This is the second telling in three verses and it has grown smoother. Lies usually do, and every retelling trains the teller a little more.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She does not throw the garment away. She lays it up by her and waits for evening and her husband's footsteps. There is a patience in falsehood that ought to make us careful, the evidence kept warm until the right hour.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To the servants she said a Hebrew; to her husband she says your servant, the Hebrew servant whom you brought to us. She knows exactly where to put the knife, in his pride, in the household he chose and staffed. It is a small detail and a very old kind of cruelty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Her speech closes the way the earlier one did, the same three beats in the same order, and the repetition does its work. A story told twice the same way sounds like truth. Meanwhile the man who actually ran is in a cell, and the man listening has not yet asked him a single question.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Potiphar's wrath is kindled, and we are not told at whom. He had trusted this steward with everything, and now his whole house is telling him he was a fool. The plain sense is that he believed his wife, and the anger fell on the innocent one, which is one of the oldest sorrows in the world.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph's master takes him and puts him in the prison where the king's prisoners were held, the place attached to the captain of the guard's own house. So the man who ran a rich estate now keeps company with Pharaoh's disgraced officials, and that turns out to be precisely the room where his future is waiting. Providence sometimes looks like a demotion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Then, with one small word, the story turns: but Yahweh was with Joseph. It is the same sentence as verse 2, spoken again over a prison instead of a fine house, which tells us the promise was never about the address. Stephen, telling this story centuries later, sums it up in four words, God was with him. Kindness and favor come this time from the keeper of the prison, and they come from the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The keeper hands over every prisoner in the place, and once more everything is put into Joseph's hand. Same phrase as Potiphar's house, same trust, same young man, only now the walls are stone. Character formed in a palace is not lost in a jail; it simply finds new work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The keeper stops checking on anything, because the man in his charge is trustworthy and because Yahweh is with him. Readers today hear an echo of every unseen back room and quiet desk where someone does good work with no audience at all, and of a God who calls that prospering. As of 2026-10, I am still learning that the Lord's presence, not the size of the room, is what makes a life flourish.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
